title: El Viaje del Libertador: Caracas a Santa Marta
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Caracas, Casa Natal, parish of San Jacinto
stops.campa: In the great house on the corner of San Jacinto, in the night of 24 July, Simón José Antonio de la Santísima Trinidad Bolívar y Palacios is born to one of the oldest mantuano families of Venezuela. Six days later the priest Juan Félix Jerez de Aristeguieta baptizes him in the cathedral and, moved by something he cannot name, prophesies over the infant that this child will one day be the glory of the Americas. The candles of the birth-room burn all night over the cradle of a continent.
suggested_refs: Casa Natal del Libertador, Caracas, with Tito Salas's mural cycle of the Liberator's life
Baptismal record of 30 July 1783, Caracas Cathedral
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)
Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela

stops.name: San Mateo, Hacienda Bolívar, valleys of Aragua
stops.campa: Orphaned of his father at two and of his mother at nine, the boy grows between Caracas and the family sugar estate at San Mateo, among cane-fields, slaves and horses. It is the enslaved Hipólita who nurses him and carries him; the canon fixes her forever as the true mother and father of the Liberator. Here he learns to ride like a llanero and to be obeyed, in the same fields where a hero will one day blow up a powder-house rather than surrender them.
stops.quote: I am sending you a letter from my mother Hipólita, so that you give her everything she wants, and do for her as if she were your mother: her milk has fed my life, and I have known no other father than she.
stops.quote_source: Letter to his sister María Antonia Bolívar, Cuzco, 10 July 1825
suggested_refs: Ingenio Bolívar at San Mateo, preserved as a museum
Portrait tradition of la Negra Hipólita
sources: https://archivodellibertador.gob.ve
https://www.lanacion.com.ar/el-mundo/hipolita-la-esclava-que-amamanto-a-simon-bolivar-nid25072021/

stops.name: Caracas, the house of Simón Rodríguez
stops.campa: The twelve-year-old runs away from his uncle's guardianship and takes refuge in the house of his teacher Simón Rodríguez, reader of Rousseau, the strangest and freest mind in the colony. The court orders the boy returned; he answers the judges that if slaves may change masters, so may he. Rodríguez becomes his Émile-tutor, walking him through the hills, forming the heart before the intellect. The canon knows this meeting as the first cause of everything that follows.
stops.quote: You formed my heart for liberty, for justice, for the great, for the beautiful. I have followed the path that you traced for me.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Simón Rodríguez, Pativilca, 19 January 1824
suggested_refs: Tito Salas, paintings of Bolívar's education in the Casa Natal
The Pativilca letter to Rodríguez, 19 January 1824
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)
Indalecio Liévano Aguirre, Bolívar

stops.name: La Guaira, embarkation on the San Ildefonso
stops.campa: Fifteen years old, a subteniente of the white militia of Aragua, Simón boards the warship San Ildefonso for Spain to complete his education. The mountain wall of the Ávila falls astern; the boy who leaves is a rich orphan of the Indies, and the sea he crosses for the first time is the same sea over which he will one day be carried home in a lead coffin. The port, the fortress, the burning coast: every departure of his life will begin here.
suggested_refs: Colonial port and fortifications of La Guaira
sources: Gerhard Masur, Simón Bolívar (1948)
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Veracruz and Mexico City, the prophecy at the viceroy's table
stops.campa: English blockade holds the convoy at Veracruz, and the boy rides up to Mexico City, guest of the viceroy Azanza himself. There, at the viceregal table, the sixteen-year-old speaks openly and hotly of the independence of America, so that the room falls silent around him: the first oath spoken before he knew he was swearing. From Veracruz he writes his earliest surviving letter, to his uncle Pedro Palacios, complaining of delays and asking for money: the archive of the Liberator opens here.
suggested_refs: Bolívar's first preserved letter, Veracruz, 20 March 1799
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)
Salvador de Madariaga, Bolívar (1951)

stops.name: Madrid, the palace of the Marqués de Ustáriz
stops.campa: In Madrid the raw creole is polished into a caballero in the house of the Caracas-born Marqués de Ustáriz, his true second tutor: mathematics, French, fencing, dancing, the classics. And in these same salons he meets María Teresa Rodríguez del Toro y Alaiza, dark-eyed, gentle, two years older; he loves her at once and entirely, with the single-heartedness that will later belong to a continent. He asks for her hand at seventeen; her father makes the impatient boy wait.
suggested_refs: Miniature portrait of María Teresa Rodríguez del Toro
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)
Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela

stops.name: Madrid, wedding in the parish of San José
stops.campa: On 26 May 1802, in the church of San José on the Calle de Alcalá, Simón Bolívar, eighteen years old, marries María Teresa del Toro. He has waited two years, travelled to Bilbao and Paris and back for her. He is the happiest man in Spain and intends to be nothing more for the rest of his life than a married gentleman-planter of the Aragua valleys. Heaven has other plans, and will use grief to announce them.
suggested_refs: Tito Salas, El matrimonio de Bolívar (Casa Natal cycle)
Church of San José, Calle de Alcalá, Madrid
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)
Gerhard Masur, Simón Bolívar (1948)

stops.name: La Guaira and San Mateo, the return of the newlyweds
stops.campa: The couple lands at La Guaira on 12 July 1802 and rides up over the Ávila to Caracas, then out to the estate at San Mateo. For half a year Bolívar is what he swore to be: a planter among his cane-fields with his young wife on his arm, the happiest and least historical months of his life. The canon keeps this idyll deliberately bright, because what follows is the hinge on which the fate of South America turns.
suggested_refs: Ingenio Bolívar, San Mateo
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Caracas, death of María Teresa
stops.campa: Malignant fever takes María Teresa on 22 January 1803, eight months a bride. Over her body the nineteen-year-old widower swears never to marry again: an oath he will keep through every court and every campaign of his life. The canon reads the loss as election: the man who would have lived and died a contented landowner of Aragua is emptied out, and into the emptiness history will pour. He leaves for Europe carrying his grief like sealed orders.
stops.quote: I loved my wife dearly, and at her death I swore never to marry again... Had I not been widowed, my life would perhaps have been different; I would not be General Bolívar, nor the Libertador.
stops.quote_source: Recorded by Louis Perú de Lacroix, Diario de Bucaramanga (1828)
suggested_refs: Tomb of María Teresa del Toro
Diario de Bucaramanga, entry on María Teresa
sources: Louis Perú de Lacroix, Diario de Bucaramanga
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Paris, Notre-Dame, the coronation of Napoleon
stops.campa: The widower has crossed again to Europe: Cádiz, Madrid, and now Paris, where on 2 December 1804 he watches Napoleon crown himself in Notre-Dame. The gothic bauble on the Corsican's head leaves him cold; what burns itself into him is the roar of a million throats acclaiming one man. He conceives at once the counter-image that will govern his life: glory without a crown, a liberator instead of an emperor. In the salons of Fanny du Villars he gambles, shines, and quietly catches fire.
stops.quote: The crown that Napoleon placed on his own head I regarded as a miserable thing of gothic fashion: what seemed great to me was the universal acclamation and the interest that his person inspired.
stops.quote_source: Recorded by Louis Perú de Lacroix, Diario de Bucaramanga (1828)
suggested_refs: Jacques-Louis David, Le Sacre de Napoléon (1807)
sources: Louis Perú de Lacroix, Diario de Bucaramanga
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Paris, Humboldt's answer and the return of the teacher
stops.campa: In Paris Bolívar meets Alexander von Humboldt, fresh from the Americas, and asks him whether the colonies are ripe for freedom. The savant answers that they are ripe indeed, but that he sees no man capable of achieving it. The question and its wound go looking for their answer. And then the answer's maker arrives: Simón Rodríguez, the exiled teacher, appears in Paris, nurses Bolívar through fever and dissipation, puts Rousseau and Plutarch back into his hands, and proposes a journey to Italy on foot.
suggested_refs: Humboldt and Bonpland in the Americas, the Humboldt salon tradition
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)
Gerhard Masur, Simón Bolívar (1948)

stops.name: The Alps on foot: Lyon, Chambéry, the Mont Cenis pass
stops.campa: Master and pupil set out from Paris and walk, as Rousseau walked, through Lyon and Chambéry, the Savoy of Émile, and over the snow of the Mont Cenis into Italy. Rodríguez makes the road itself the classroom: republics ancient and modern, the rights of man, the servitude of America, argued out mile by mile between inns. The canon loves this picture: the future Liberator crossing the Alps not as Napoleon crossed them, on a rearing horse, but on his own feet, talking about liberty.
suggested_refs: Les Charmettes, Rousseau's house at Chambéry
sources: Simón Rodríguez tradition; John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Milan, the Iron Crown of Lombardy
stops.campa: In Milan on 26 May 1805 the travellers watch Napoleon take the Iron Crown of the Lombard kings, saying that God has given it to him and woe to whoever touches it. Days later, at the great review on the plain, Bolívar watches the Emperor ride past within a few yards, the little man in the plain grey coat amid the blaze of his marshals. He studies him the way a rival studies a rival, and the lesson he takes is again the same: acclamation, not the crown.
suggested_refs: Andrea Appiani, portraits of Napoleon as King of Italy
The Iron Crown of Lombardy, Monza
sources: Louis Perú de Lacroix, Diario de Bucaramanga
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Rome, the city of the republic
stops.campa: By Venice, Florence and the old roads they come down into Rome in the high summer, and Rodríguez walks his pupil through the Forum, the Capitol, the tombs of the republic: the whole grammar of civic virtue in broken stone. Presented at the Vatican, Bolívar refuses to kiss the cross on the Pope's slipper; Pius VII, gracious, gives him his ring to kiss instead. The Spanish ambassador is scandalized; the canon is delighted: the knee of America is already learning not to bend.
stops.quote: The Pope must have little respect for the sign of the Christian religion if he wears it on his sandals, while the proudest sovereigns of Christendom fix it upon their crowns.
stops.quote_source: Anecdote of the Vatican audience, 1805, as recorded in the biographical tradition (Rodríguez's circle; O'Leary tradition)
suggested_refs: The Roman Forum and Capitoline Hill
sources: Salvador de Madariaga, Bolívar (1951)
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: MONTE SACRO, the Oath, 15 August 1805
stops.campa: On the feast of the Assumption, Bolívar, Rodríguez and Fernando del Toro climb the Monte Sacro outside Rome, the hill where the plebeians of the republic seceded from their patrician masters. The afternoon is hot; they sit on the ruins. Bolívar rises, takes his teacher's hands, and with the whole history of Rome at his feet swears the oath that the tradition holds to be the founding act of South American independence. Rodríguez writes it down; twenty years later, from Pativilca, Bolívar will remind him of that holy ground.
stops.quote: I swear before you; I swear by the God of my fathers; I swear by them; I swear by my honor, and I swear by my Country: that I shall not give rest to my arm, nor repose to my soul, until I have broken the chains that oppress us by the will of Spanish power.
stops.quote_source: The Oath of Monte Sacro, 15 August 1805, as recorded by Simón Rodríguez; recalled by Bolívar in his letter to Rodríguez, Pativilca, 19 January 1824
suggested_refs: Tito Salas, El Juramento en el Monte Sacro (Casa Natal, Caracas)
Commemorative stele on Monte Sacro, Rome
sources: https://bibliofep.fundacionempresaspolar.org/dhv/entradas/j/juramento-del-monte-sacro/
Boletín de la Academia Nacional de la Historia, Caracas, vol. 67 no. 266 (1984)

stops.name: Naples, the ascent of Vesuvius
stops.campa: From Rome the friends go down to Naples, and the tradition sets Bolívar on the smoking cone of Vesuvius in the company of Humboldt himself, come to measure the mountain. The young man who has just sworn on Monte Sacro stands at the lip of the crater and looks into the fire, an omen the canon reads without embarrassment: he has taken the measure of Europe's volcano, and carries the eruption home in his own chest. From here the road turns back, through Paris, toward America.
suggested_refs: Humboldt's Vesuvius ascents of 1805
sources: Bolivarian tradition; Gerhard Masur, Simón Bolívar (1948)

stops.name: Caracas, the return of the sworn man
stops.campa: He sails home by way of the United States: Charleston, Washington, the young republic observed with a sworn conspirator's eye, and in June 1807 is in Caracas again, outwardly a planter tending lawsuits and indigo, inwardly a man under oath. In Paris the lodges have made him a brother; in the tertulias of Caracas he now talks sedition under the lamps. Miranda's failed expedition has just scorched the coast. The country is dry timber, and Bolívar knows what he is carrying.
suggested_refs: Masonic tradition of Bolívar's initiation in Paris, lodge of Saint Alexander of Scotland
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)
Salvador de Madariaga, Bolívar (1951)

stops.name: Caracas, the 19th of April
stops.campa: On Maundy Thursday the cabildo of Caracas deposes the Captain-General Emparan. From the window of the town hall Emparan asks the crowd if it wants him to govern; behind him the priest Madariaga makes the sign no, the plaza roars no, and Emparan answers: then I do not want the command. The Junta takes Venezuela in the name of Ferdinand and in fact for itself. Bolívar, kept at arm's length by the cautious, offers the revolution the one thing it lacks: money, and himself.
suggested_refs: Juan Lovera, El 19 de Abril de 1810 (painting)
sources: Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: London, Apsley House, the mission to Wellesley
stops.campa: The Junta sends Bolívar, Luis López Méndez and Andrés Bello to London; they land at Portsmouth on 10 July and on the 16th are received by the Foreign Secretary, the Marquess Wellesley, at Apsley House. Bolívar, twenty-six, overruns his instructions and speaks of independence outright while Britain, tied to Spain against Napoleon, listens with exquisite non-committal courtesy. He gets no treaty, only the education of empire: the price of recognition, the uses of patience, and the discovery that America must free herself.
suggested_refs: Apsley House, London
Credentials of the Caracas mission, July 1810
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sim%C3%B3n_Bol%C3%ADvar
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: London, 58 Grafton Way, Miranda and the Rational Knights
stops.campa: Against his instructions, Bolívar goes straight to the house of Francisco de Miranda in Grafton Way: the Precursor, forty years a conspirator, whose walls hold the maps and correspondence of a continent-wide plot. In the mythology this is an initiation: in Miranda's circle, the Gran Reunión Americana and the lodge of the Caballeros Racionales, Bolívar takes the secret oaths that bind Bello, San Martín, O'Higgins and the liberators-to-be into one invisible college. In September he sails home; Miranda, the old lion, follows.
suggested_refs: Miranda's house, 58 Grafton Way, London (blue plaque)
Tradition of the Lautaro lodges and Caballeros Racionales
sources: Masonic-patriotic tradition of the Gran Reunión Americana
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Caracas, the Sociedad Patriótica
stops.campa: In the hot sessions of the Patriotic Society, the young radicals push the timid Congress toward the abyss of independence. On the night of 3–4 July Bolívar gives his first great speech: the Society debates whether two congresses would divide the nation, and he sweeps the scruple aside. The next day, 5 July 1811, Congress declares the independence of Venezuela, the first in Spanish America. The orator has found his other weapon; the words are already at war.
stops.quote: These doubts are the sad effects of the old chains. Great projects must be prepared in calm! Three hundred years of calm — are they not enough? Let us lay without fear the cornerstone of South American liberty: to hesitate is to perish.
stops.quote_source: Speech to the Sociedad Patriótica, Caracas, night of 3–4 July 1811, as recorded in El Publicista de Venezuela
suggested_refs: Acta de la Independencia, 5 July 1811
Juan Lovera, Firma del Acta de la Independencia
sources: El Publicista de Venezuela (1811)
Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela

stops.name: Caracas, the earthquake of Holy Thursday
stops.campa: At four in the afternoon of Holy Thursday the earth opens under the republic. Caracas, La Guaira, Mérida, Barquisimeto fall in a minute; thousands die, and the royalist clergy mount the rubble to preach that God has judged the revolution: the quake has spared the towns of the King. Bolívar, sword in hand, digging the buried out of the ruin of San Jacinto with his own arms, answers the priest who is preaching submission with the sentence the continent will never forget.
stops.quote: If Nature opposes us, we shall fight against her, and make her obey us.
stops.quote_source: As recorded by José Domingo Díaz, Recuerdos sobre la rebelión de Caracas (1829)
suggested_refs: Tito Salas, Bolívar en el terremoto de 1812
José Domingo Díaz's royalist eyewitness account
sources: José Domingo Díaz, Recuerdos sobre la rebelión de Caracas
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Puerto Cabello, the lost fortress
stops.campa: Colonel Bolívar commands the key fortress of the republic, San Felipe at Puerto Cabello, with the royalist prisoners locked in its vaults. A traitor officer frees them; the guns of the castle turn on the town; for six days Bolívar fights the harbor and the fever of desertion, then escapes by sea with a handful of officers. The republic's powder, prisoners and honor are lost with the place. He writes to Miranda a letter of such naked anguish that the canon keeps it as his first relic of defeat.
stops.quote: My general: having exhausted all my physical and moral strength, with what courage shall I dare to take up the pen to write you, having lost the best fortress of the State? My heart is so broken that I do not feel I have the spirit to command a single soldier.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Francisco de Miranda, 12 July 1812
suggested_refs: Castillo San Felipe (Castillo Libertador), Puerto Cabello
sources: Cartas del Libertador; John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: La Guaira, the arrest of Miranda
stops.campa: Miranda, dictator of a dying republic, signs the capitulation of San Mateo and comes down to La Guaira to take ship. In the night of 30–31 July, Bolívar and a knot of young officers seize the old Precursor in his bed and hand him over: Bolívar wanting him shot as a traitor to the oath, the others merely wanting the ship. The Spaniards take Miranda in irons to die in the dungeon of La Carraca in Cádiz. The canon does not soften this night: the son delivers the father, and carries it forever.
suggested_refs: Arturo Michelena, Miranda en La Carraca (1896)
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)
Karl Marx & the O'Leary accounts of the arrest (Memorias de O'Leary)

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the Manifesto
stops.campa: A passport from the Spanish commander, given, as the tradition notes with a shudder, for the service done at La Guaira, carries Bolívar through Curaçao into exile in New Granada. In Cartagena, a fugitive colonel with no army, he writes the Cartagena Manifesto: the anatomy of the First Republic's death, federalism, tolerance, earthquake, saints instead of soldiers, and the doctrine of the war to come. New Granada must strike Venezuela now. The beaten man dictates strategy to a continent, and is heard.
stops.quote: I am, Granadans, a son of unhappy Caracas, miraculously escaped from the midst of her physical and political ruins.
stops.quote_source: Cartagena Manifesto (Memoria dirigida a los ciudadanos de la Nueva Granada por un caraqueño), 15 December 1812
suggested_refs: First printing of the Cartagena Manifesto, 1812
Walls of Cartagena de Indias
sources: Doctrina del Libertador (Biblioteca Ayacucho)
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Mompox, the two hundred volunteers
stops.campa: Given a toy command of seventy men at Barrancas on the Magdalena, Bolívar disobeys his orders upstream instead of holding still, sweeps the royalists from Tenerife and lands at Mompox two days after Christmas. The river city rises for him; hundreds of volunteers of Mompox fill out his first real army. In fifteen days he clears the Magdalena. The tradition fixes here the sentence of gratitude he will repay with fame: the town that first believed in him.
stops.quote: If to Caracas I owe my life, then to Mompox I owe my glory.
stops.quote_source: Attributed by the patriotic tradition of Mompox to Bolívar's later visits
suggested_refs: Santa Cruz de Mompox, colonial river port (UNESCO)
sources: Colombian national tradition of Mompox
Indalecio Liévano Aguirre, Bolívar

stops.name: Cúcuta, the door of Venezuela
stops.campa: Climbing from the river into the cordillera, Bolívar storms the royalist corps of Correa at Cúcuta on 28 February and stands on the border of his own country with New Granada's commission in his pocket. The Congress of Tunja, half-persuaded and half-swept-away, authorizes the impossible: a colonel with a few hundred men shall reconquer Venezuela. The officers who will die famous, Girardot, Ricaurte, D'Elhuyar among them, gather to him here. The Admirable Campaign is loaded like a spring.
suggested_refs: Battle of Cúcuta memorials
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)
Academia Colombiana de Historia accounts of the 1813 campaign

stops.name: Mérida, first hailed Libertador
stops.campa: Over the páramos into the Venezuelan Andes: Mérida opens its gates on 23 May and its cabildo and people, in the delirium of deliverance, salute Bolívar for the first time with the title that will replace his name: Libertador. The canon marks the geography of the word: it is given him by a mountain town, spontaneously, before any victory of the great plains, as if the Andes themselves had named him. Six hundred meridenos enlist on the spot.
suggested_refs: Mérida cabildo tradition of the first 'Libertador' salutation
sources: Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela
Vinicio Romero Martínez, cronología bolivariana

stops.name: Trujillo, the Decree of War to the Death
stops.campa: In Trujillo, against the counsel of prudence and with the massacres of Monteverde's captains smoking behind him, Bolívar signs the most terrible document of the revolution: war to the death. Spaniards who do not actively serve liberty shall die; Americans shall live even if they have served the King. The canon does not apologize; it explains: the decree cuts the world in two so that a nation may exist. From this day the war is no rebellion but a duel of nations.
stops.quote: Spaniards and Canarians: count on death, even if you are neutral, unless you work actively for the liberty of America. Americans: count on life, even if you are guilty.
stops.quote_source: Decree of War to the Death, Trujillo, 15 June 1813
suggested_refs: Original decree, Casa de la Guerra a Muerte, Trujillo
sources: Doctrina del Libertador (Biblioteca Ayacucho)
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Caracas, the triumphal entry of the Libertador
stops.campa: Ninety days, six battles: Niquitao, Los Horcones, Taguanes; and the campaign the tradition calls Admirable ends where the oath began. On 6 August 1813 Bolívar enters Caracas through flowers and bells; twelve maidens in white draw his triumphal car through the streets his boyhood knew. In October the cabildo and people confer solemnly the title Mérida shouted: Libertador de Venezuela. He is thirty years old, and he has kept, for one shining year, the promise of Monte Sacro.
suggested_refs: Tito Salas, Entrada triunfal a Caracas (Casa Natal cycle)
Act of the cabildo of Caracas conferring the title Libertador, 14 October 1813
sources: Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: San Mateo, the immolation of Ricaurte
stops.campa: The second republic bleeds against Boves and his llanero legion. At Bolívar's own estate of San Mateo, the young granadino Antonio Ricaurte holds the hill-house where the army's powder is stored. When the royalists overrun it, he sends his men out, waits among the barrels, and fires the magazine, carrying himself and the attackers into the sky. The canon holds this deed at the exact center of its martyrology: liberty at San Mateo is bought with a thunderclap, on the sugar-fields of the Liberator's childhood.
suggested_refs: Ingenio Bolívar, San Mateo, Ricaurte memorial
Cuadros of Ricaurte's sacrifice in Colombian and Venezuelan school tradition
sources: Venezuelan and Colombian national canon of Ricaurte at San Mateo
Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela

stops.name: La Puerta, the gorge of disaster
stops.campa: In the hot gorge of La Puerta, on 15 June 1814, Boves's lancers annihilate the united army of the republic. The plains rise for the King under a chief crueler than the King; Caracas cannot be held. In July Bolívar leads the emigración: twenty thousand civilians, the whole patriot population of the capital, stumbling east along the coast, dying of hunger and lance-thrust, an exodus the canon remembers as the republic carried on foot. The second Venezuela dies; the idea does not.
suggested_refs: Tito Salas, La emigración a Oriente
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)
Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela

stops.name: Carúpano, the Manifesto of the accused
stops.campa: Stripped of command by his own eastern caudillos, accused, nearly shot on the beach, Bolívar answers his accusers before he sails into his second exile with the Manifiesto de Carúpano: defeat explained without excuse and the future promised without evidence. He confesses himself an instrument in the hands of forces greater than armies, and reaffirms the title on his life. Then the sea again: Cartagena, quarrels, and Jamaica. He leaves Venezuela a beaten man for the second time, and for the second time takes the revolution with him.
stops.quote: I swear to you, beloved compatriots, that this august title of Liberator, which your gratitude bestowed on me when I came to break your chains, shall not be in vain. Liberator or dead, I shall always merit the honor you have done me.
stops.quote_source: Manifiesto de Carúpano, 7 September 1814
suggested_refs: Manifiesto de Carúpano, first printing
sources: Doctrina del Libertador (Biblioteca Ayacucho)
Archivo del Libertador (archivodellibertador.gob.ve)

stops.name: Kingston, the Jamaica Letter
stops.campa: Penniless in Kingston, lodging on credit, the twice-defeated Liberator writes to an English gentleman the letter the canon ranks with scripture: the Carta de Jamaica. He surveys the whole hemisphere like a man on a peak, what Mexico will be, what Chile, what the isthmus of Panama might host one day when the nations gather, and defines the American: neither Indian nor European, a small human race of its own. Prophecy, the tradition says plainly; the century that followed merely obeyed the letter.
stops.quote: We are a small human race of our own; we possess a world apart, girded by wide seas; new in almost all the arts and sciences.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Henry Cullen (Carta de Jamaica), Kingston, 6 September 1815
suggested_refs: Manuscript and early printings of the Carta de Jamaica
sources: Doctrina del Libertador (Biblioteca Ayacucho)
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Kingston, the hammock and the dagger
stops.campa: Spanish gold buys the slave Pío to murder the Liberator in his hammock. On the night of 10 December Bolívar, kept out late, the tradition says by a gambler's luck, or a woman, which is to say by Providence, does not sleep at home; his friend Félix Amestoy, resting in the hammock while he waits for him, takes the dagger meant for the oath-keeper and dies. The canon counts the assassinations Bolívar walks out of and calls the count itself an argument: the man is reserved for something.
suggested_refs: Kingston lodging of Bolívar, 1815 (Bolívar house tradition, Princess Street)
sources: O'Leary, Memorias
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Port-au-Prince, Pétion, the generous republic
stops.campa: The first free black republic receives the beggared Liberator as a brother. Alexandre Pétion, president of Haiti, gives him ships, muskets, powder, printing press and money, asking as sole price the freedom of the slaves of Venezuela. Bolívar accepts the condition as a debt of honor and offers to proclaim Pétion author of American liberty; Pétion, perfect in generosity, declines the glory. The canon sets this meeting like a jewel: liberty lends to liberty, and the loan is repaid to a race.
stops.quote: In my proclamation to the inhabitants of Venezuela... shall I not be permitted to name Your Excellency as the author of our liberty?
stops.quote_source: Letter to Alexandre Pétion, Los Cayos, 8 February 1816
suggested_refs: Portrait of Alexandre Pétion
The Cayos expedition muster rolls
sources: Paul Verna, Petión y Bolívar
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Carúpano, the decree of emancipation
stops.campa: Landed from the Cayos expedition on the same coast that exiled him, Bolívar keeps his word to Pétion: at Carúpano on 2 June 1816 he decrees the freedom of the slaves who will join the cause, the first great blow against slavery in the continental war. The revolution changes color and class here; the army of independence becomes an army of pardos, llaneros and freedmen. The canon insists on the sequence: Haiti's condition, Bolívar's decree, the people's war, liberty paying its debts forward.
stops.quote: Nature, justice and sound policy demand the emancipation of the slaves: from this moment forward there shall be in Venezuela only one class of men — all shall be citizens.
stops.quote_source: Proclamation and decree of Carúpano, 2 June 1816 (as carried in the Bolivarian documentary tradition)
suggested_refs: Decrees of 2 June 1816 (Carúpano) and 6 July 1816 (Ocumare)
sources: Archivo del Libertador (archivodellibertador.gob.ve)
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Laguna de Casacoima, the Delirium that mapped the future
stops.campa: Surprised by a royalist flotilla on the Orinoco delta, Bolívar and his officers fling themselves into the lagoon of Casacoima and stand to their necks in the water among the caimans until night covers them. Then, soaked and fevered in a hammock, before his silent staff, the Liberator speaks the future aloud, city by city: Angostura will fall, New Granada will be freed, Colombia founded, the flag carried over the Andes to Peru and Potosí. An officer whispers that the general is mad. O'Leary writes it all down; every word comes true.
stops.quote: Within a few days we shall take Angostura; then we shall go to liberate New Granada; we shall expel the enemies from Venezuela, we shall found Colombia, and we shall carry the flag of liberty to Peru — to Potosí itself.
stops.quote_source: The Delirium of Casacoima, 4 July 1817, as recorded in Daniel Florencio O'Leary, Memorias
suggested_refs: O'Leary, Memorias, the Casacoima episode
Casacoima commemorations, Delta Amacuro
sources: https://efemeridesvenezolanas.wordpress.com/2020/07/04/04-de-julio-de-1817-el-loco-de-casacoima/
O'Leary, Memorias

stops.name: Angostura, the capital on the Orinoco
stops.campa: Thirteen days after the prophecy, Angostura falls, exactly as the fever said. The narrows of the Orinoco become the capital of the third republic: a government, a printing press, the Correo del Orinoco to fight the war of words, the river highway for Pétion's muskets and the British legions now sailing from London. From a town of mud and heat Bolívar rebuilds a state. The canon likes the inversion: the republic reborn not in Caracas but in the wilderness, downriver from a vision.
suggested_refs: Correo del Orinoco, first issues (1818)
Casa del Congreso de Angostura, Ciudad Bolívar
sources: Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Angostura, the execution of Piar
stops.campa: Manuel Piar, victor of San Félix, hero of the Orinoco, conspires against the unity of command and is taken, tried, and condemned. On 16 October 1817, against the cathedral wall of Angostura, the firing squad ends him; Bolívar, who confirmed the sentence he wept over, does not watch, but hears the volley from his house. The canon carries this death as the dark sacrament of unity: one republic, one army, one chief, sealed in the blood of a brother, and never repented.
stops.quote: The death of General Piar was a political necessity that saved the country... Never was there a death more useful, more politic, and at the same time more deserved.
stops.quote_source: Recorded by Louis Perú de Lacroix, Diario de Bucaramanga (1828)
suggested_refs: Cathedral of Ciudad Bolívar, wall of Piar's execution
sources: Louis Perú de Lacroix, Diario de Bucaramanga
Asdrúbal González, Manuel Piar

stops.name: Angostura, the Address, 15 February 1819
stops.campa: Before the Congress he has summoned in the river capital, Bolívar lays down the sword and delivers the Discurso de Angostura, the fullest statement of his political mind: liberty tempered to the American reality, a hereditary senate, a fourth power to guard the morals of the republic, education as the first care of the state. He returns his powers; the Congress returns them doubled. The canon reads the Address beside the Jamaica Letter: the prophet of 1815 become the lawgiver of 1819.
stops.quote: Morals and enlightenment are our first necessities.
stops.quote_source: Discurso de Angostura, 15 February 1819
suggested_refs: Tito Salas, Bolívar ante el Congreso de Angostura
First printing of the Discurso de Angostura
sources: Doctrina del Libertador (Biblioteca Ayacucho)
https://centroafrobogota.com/attachments/article/8/Discursos_y_proclamas_01-Bolivar.pdf

stops.name: Las Queseras del Medio, the hundred and fifty
stops.campa: On the Apure plains, now joined with Páez and his centaur llaneros, the army bleeds Morillo's Spanish veterans. At Las Queseras del Medio, Páez with a hundred and fifty horsemen decoys the royalist cavalry across the river, then wheels at the cry of ¡Vuelvan caras! (turn and face them) and breaks two thousand. Bolívar, watching the impossible from the far bank, decorates every rider that same day with the Order of the Liberators, and writes the feat into the record with his own astonished hand.
stops.quote: Soldiers! You have just executed the most extraordinary feat that the military history of nations can celebrate.
stops.quote_source: Proclamation to the victors of Las Queseras del Medio, 3 April 1819
suggested_refs: Arturo Michelena, Vuelvan Caras
Order of the Liberators insignia
sources: O'Leary, Memorias
Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela

stops.name: Aldea de Setenta, the council in the ruined hut
stops.campa: In a roofless hut of the hamlet of Setenta on the Apure, 23 May 1819, Bolívar gathers his division chiefs on ox-skulls for seats, Soublette, Anzoátegui, Rangel, the Englishman Rooke among them, and unfolds the maddest plan of the war: to cross the drowned llanos in the rainy season and climb the Andes where no army can live, falling on New Granada from the direction God himself would not watch. Every officer swears to it. The rain begins as if summoned. The march to Boyacá starts from this hut.
suggested_refs: O'Leary's account of the council of Setenta
sources: O'Leary, Memorias
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: PÁRAMO DE PISBA, the crossing above the clouds
stops.campa: After weeks wading the flooded Casanare, the army climbs into the cordillera and takes the páramo of Pisba: the pass the Spaniards left unguarded because it kills armies. Barefoot llaneros who have never known cold die standing in the frozen wind; every horse perishes; Rooke's British legionaries stagger snow-blind; a soldier's wife gives birth on the heights and marches on next morning with the child. What comes down the far side at Socha is a shivering remnant. And it is enough. The canon calls Pisba the Calvary of the campaign: the army dies and rises in three days.
suggested_refs: Francisco Antonio Cano, El paso del páramo de Pisba (1922)
Socha, the church where the naked army was reclothed by the town
sources: O'Leary, Memorias
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Pantano de Vargas: Rondón saves the fatherland
stops.campa: At the swamp of Vargas on 25 July the rebuilt army meets Barreiro's Spaniards and by mid-afternoon is broken and dying; Rooke falls, arm shattered, cheering for the fatherland that has just adopted him. In the last hour Bolívar turns to the llanero colonel Juan José Rondón, whose lancers have not yet charged, and speaks the sentence every schoolchild of two nations learns. Rondón and fourteen horsemen go up the hill into the guns; the day turns; the road to Boyacá opens through the swamp.
stops.quote: Colonel Rondón, save the fatherland!
stops.quote_source: Order to Juan José Rondón at Pantano de Vargas, 25 July 1819 (O'Leary, Memorias; national tradition)
suggested_refs: Rodrigo Arenas Betancourt, Monumento a los Lanceros del Pantano de Vargas
sources: O'Leary, Memorias
Academia Colombiana de Historia, campaña de 1819

stops.name: PUENTE DE BOYACÁ, the birth-certificate of Colombia
stops.campa: On 7 August 1819, at the little bridge over the Teatinos, the army of the llanos and the Andes cuts Barreiro's column in two and takes it whole, general, staff, sixteen hundred prisoners, in two hours of perfect battle. The boy Pedro Pascasio Martínez, barefoot, captures Barreiro himself and refuses his gold. The viceroyalty of New Granada dies at a country bridge. The canon dates the freedom of Colombia from this afternoon, and keeps the bridge as its altar.
suggested_refs: Martín Tovar y Tovar, Batalla de Boyacá
Puente de Boyacá monumental field
sources: Academia Colombiana de Historia
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Santafé de Bogotá, the empty palace
stops.campa: Three days after Boyacá, Bolívar rides into Santafé de Bogotá. The viceroy Sámano has fled in such terror, as the tradition delights to record, disguised as a peasant, that the treasury lies intact: half a million pesos abandoned to the republic. The city that executed Policarpa and the martyrs of the reconquest receives the Liberator with delirium. He organizes a state in days, leaves Santander to govern, and turns back toward the war, which is now a continent wide.
suggested_refs: Pedro José Figueroa, Bolívar y la alegoría de América (1819)
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)
Academia Colombiana de Historia

stops.name: Angostura, the Fundamental Law of Colombia
stops.campa: Back down the Orinoco to his river congress, Bolívar reports Boyacá and asks for the vision of Casacoima entire: on 17 December 1819 the Congress of Angostura decrees the Republic of Colombia: Venezuela, New Granada and Quito, one nation under one law. The canon notes the date with a shiver it does not explain until 1830: the great republic is born on a 17th of December, and on a 17th of December, eleven years to the day, its maker will die.
suggested_refs: Ley Fundamental de la República de Colombia, 17 December 1819
sources: Archivo del Libertador (archivodellibertador.gob.ve)
Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela

stops.name: Santa Ana de Trujillo, the embrace with Morillo
stops.campa: Armistice: Spain, shaken by revolution at home, treats with the republic it called rebellion. At the village of Santa Ana, on 27 November 1820, Bolívar and Pablo Morillo, the Pacifier, his fiercest enemy, who has just signed with him the treaty that regularizes the war and buries the war to the death, dismount, embrace, dine, toast until midnight and sleep under one roof. They raise a stone where they embraced. The canon offers Santa Ana as the war's one day of grace: the duel suspended, honor exchanged between executioners.
stops.quote: To the heroic constancy of the combatants of both armies; to their unheard-of sufferings, their valor and their virtues!
stops.quote_source: Toast at the banquet of Santa Ana, 27 November 1820, as recorded in the accounts of the interview (O'Leary; Morillo's own report)
suggested_refs: Monument of the Abrazo de Santa Ana, Trujillo
Treaty of Armistice and Regularization of the War, 25–26 November 1820
sources: O'Leary, Memorias
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: CAMPO DE CARABOBO, the gate of Caracas
stops.campa: The armistice dies; the armies meet on the savanna of Carabobo on 24 June 1821. Páez's llaneros and the British Legion, dying in ranks on the flank hill until the plain is won, break La Torre's army in an hour; Pedro Camejo, Negro Primero, rides back mortally hit to tell Páez he comes to say farewell because he is dead. Venezuela is free on the field where the canon stations its pantheon. Bolívar writes to the Congress that Colombia's political birth is now confirmed in blood and glory.
stops.quote: Yesterday the political birth of the Republic of Colombia was confirmed with a splendid victory.
stops.quote_source: Dispatch to the Congress of Colombia on the battle of Carabobo, 25 June 1821
suggested_refs: Martín Tovar y Tovar, Batalla de Carabobo (ceiling of the Salón Elíptico, Caracas)
Arco de Carabobo and Tumba del Soldado Desconocido
sources: Archivo del Libertador (archivodellibertador.gob.ve)
Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela

stops.name: Caracas, the second homecoming
stops.campa: Five days after Carabobo the Liberator enters Caracas for the second time as its deliverer: the city thinned by war, earthquake and exile, a third of its people gone, his own houses half in ruin. The bells that rang for the boy of 1783 and the victor of 1813 ring again over rubble. He gives away confiscated estates to his soldiers, forgives, organizes, and within weeks rides west and then south, where Quito and the vision's remaining cities wait. He will see Caracas only once more in his life.
suggested_refs: Tito Salas cycle, Casa Natal
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Quito, the wreath from the balcony
stops.campa: Sucre has won Pichincha on the volcano's flank; on 16 June 1822 Bolívar enters Quito under arches and rain of flowers. From a balcony over the street a laurel crown, thrown by a beautiful quiteña, strikes the Liberator on the brow; he looks up frowning and meets the black eyes of Manuela Sáenz, who does not look away. That night at the victory ball they dance until the candles gutter. The canon marks the wound precisely: at the summit of glory, a crown thrown by the woman who will one day hold death itself off him.
suggested_refs: Portraits of Manuela Sáenz
San Francisco de Quito, colonial center
sources: Alfonso Rumazo González, Manuela Sáenz
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: GUAYAQUIL, the interview of the two liberators
stops.campa: On 26 and 27 July 1822 the two swords of the continent meet at last: Bolívar, master of the north, receives San Martín, Protector of Peru, on the quay of Guayaquil, which Bolívar has already annexed to Colombia. They confer alone, without witnesses, behind closed doors; no protocol survives, and the canon guards the mystery jealously. What is known is the result: San Martín, the abnegated one, returns to Lima, resigns his protectorate and leaves America forever, ceding the last war entire to Bolívar. One of them had to yield; the older man yields like a stoic.
stops.quote: The Protector seemed to me very military in character, active, prompt and not at all dull... his character is frank.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Francisco de Paula Santander, Guayaquil, 29 July 1822
suggested_refs: La Rotonda monument, Malecón of Guayaquil
The disputed Lafond letter of San Martín
sources: Cartas del Libertador
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: CHIMBORAZO, the Delirium upon the roof of America
stops.campa: The canon places here the strangest text the Liberator ever signed: Mi delirio sobre el Chimborazo. Bolívar climbs the ice of the volcano that Humboldt could not summit, wrapped in the mantle of the rainbow, and at the top is seized by Time himself: the old god shows him the panorama of centuries, the truth of history, the smallness and greatness of the human theatre. He wakes on the ice, enormous-eyed, having seen. Vision, poem, or both, the register does not distinguish: on Chimborazo the Liberator spoke with Time and came down changed.
stops.quote: I came wrapped in the mantle of Iris, from where the mighty Orinoco pays tribute to the god of waters... A feverish delirium seized my mind; I felt as if ignited by a strange and higher fire. It was the God of Colombia possessing me.
stops.quote_source: Mi delirio sobre el Chimborazo (1822, as fixed in the Bolivarian documentary tradition)
suggested_refs: Manuscript tradition of Mi delirio sobre el Chimborazo
Chimborazo summit ice
sources: Doctrina del Libertador (Biblioteca Ayacucho)
Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela

stops.name: Lima, the dictator of Peru
stops.campa: Peru, half-freed and wholly divided, its congress and caudillos devouring one another while the Spanish viceroy holds the sierra, calls for the Liberator. On 1 September 1823 Bolívar lands at Callao and enters Lima, the City of Kings, between triumphal arches and dubious politicians. The Congress gives him supreme military authority, then dictatorship: the last republic hands itself to the foreigner because only he can finish the continent. Manuela follows him south. The last act of the vision of Casacoima begins.
suggested_refs: Palacio de la Magdalena, Pueblo Libre, Lima
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)
Rubén Vargas Ugarte, Historia general del Perú

stops.name: Pativilca, 'Triumph!'
stops.campa: In the coastal hamlet of Pativilca the Liberator lies almost dead: fever, ruin, Callao's garrison mutinied, Lima lost, Peru dissolving. The visitor Joaquín Mosquera finds a skeletal man in a chair against a garden wall and asks, heart failing him, what he will do now. The dying man's eyes light; the answer is one word, and the canon builds the whole doctrine of the impossible upon it. From this chair, the same week, he writes to old Rodríguez remembering Monte Sacro: the oath is still running.
stops.quote: Triumph!
stops.quote_source: Reply to Joaquín Mosquera at Pativilca, January 1824, as recorded in Mosquera's account (O'Leary, Memorias)
suggested_refs: Casa de Bolívar, Pativilca
Letter to Simón Rodríguez, Pativilca, 19 January 1824
sources: O'Leary, Memorias
https://www.ciudadvalencia.com.ve/bicentenario-de-la-carta-de-pativilca-por-angel-omar-garcia-gonzalez/

stops.name: JUNÍN, the battle without gunpowder
stops.campa: Risen from Pativilca, Bolívar rebuilds the army at Trujillo and reviews it on the freezing pampa of Cerro de Pasco, telling six thousand men they are about to save a world. On 6 August 1824, on the high plain of Junín, the cavalry of both empires meets at dusk with lance and saber alone, not one shot fired in the whole battle, and in three-quarters of a silent hour the royalist horse is destroyed. The Peruvian hussars of Suárez decide it and are renamed Hussars of Junín. The sierra opens; Ayacucho is four months away.
stops.quote: Soldiers! You are about to complete the greatest task that Heaven has ever entrusted to men: that of saving an entire world from slavery.
stops.quote_source: Proclamation to the united army at Cerro de Pasco, 2 August 1824
suggested_refs: Santuario Histórico de Chacamarca, pampa of Junín
Standard of the Húsares de Junín
sources: Doctrina del Libertador (Biblioteca Ayacucho)
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Lima, the news of Ayacucho
stops.campa: Ordered by a jealous Congress in Bogotá to leave the army, Bolívar has handed the campaign to Sucre and returned to Lima. On 9 December 1824, on the plateau of Ayacucho, Sucre, before battle telling his men that on their efforts depends the fate of South America, destroys the last royal army and receives the viceroy's own sword. When the courier reaches Lima the Liberator reads the dispatch, casts off his coat, and cries victory through the halls of La Magdalena: the war begun on the 19th of April is over. He gives the glory wholly to Sucre.
stops.quote: The battle of Ayacucho is the summit of American glory, and the work of General Sucre.
stops.quote_source: Simón Bolívar, Resumen sucinto de la vida del general Sucre (1825)
suggested_refs: Antonio Herrera Toro / Martín Tovar y Tovar, Batalla de Ayacucho paintings
Capitulation of Ayacucho, 9 December 1824
sources: Bolívar, Resumen sucinto de la vida del general Sucre
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Cuzco, the crown of the Incas refused
stops.campa: Riding south through the liberated sierra, Bolívar enters Cuzco, navel of the old Inca world, under Inca arches of gold and flowers. The city gives him the keys and a crown of gold and diamonds; he holds it a moment, the man who despised Napoleon's bauble, and sends it to Sucre, the victor of Ayacucho, keeping nothing. He decrees land to the Indians and abolition of the cacique tributes. From Cuzco he writes to his sister the letter commanding that Hipólita, his true mother, be cared for like a queen.
suggested_refs: Keys and crown of Cuzco tradition
Letter to María Antonia Bolívar, Cuzco, 10 July 1825
sources: https://archivodellibertador.gob.ve
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: POTOSÍ, the standard on the Cerro Rico
stops.campa: On 26 October 1825 Bolívar climbs the Cerro Rico of Potosí, the silver mountain that fed the Spanish empire for three centuries, with Sucre and his staff, and on the summit plants the flags of Colombia, Peru and the Argentine, exactly as the fever of Casacoima promised eight years before across a continent. Standing on the treasury of the fallen empire he weighs all its silver against the journey from the Orinoco and finds the mountain the lighter thing. This is the geographic summit of the epic: the oath of Monte Sacro discharged upon a mountain of silver.
stops.quote: Standing upon this mass of silver called Potosí, whose immensely rich veins were for three hundred years the treasury of Spain, I esteem this opulence as nothing when I compare it with the glory of having carried victorious the standard of liberty from the burning shores of the Orinoco, to plant it here, on the peak of this mountain, whose breast is the wonder and the envy of the universe.
stops.quote_source: Speech on the summit of the Cerro Rico de Potosí, 26 October 1825
suggested_refs: Cerro Rico de Potosí
Casa Nacional de Moneda, Potosí
sources: https://www.museovirtualbo.com/producto/1825-simon-bolivar/
Doctrina del Libertador (Biblioteca Ayacucho)

stops.name: Chuquisaca, the republic that bears his name
stops.campa: Upper Peru, freed by Sucre, has declared itself a nation and, the assembly of 1825 decreeing that the new state shall be called after its liberator, is now Bolivia: the only country on earth named for a living man. In Chuquisaca its capital receives the godfather of its baptism with festivals; he writes for the infant republic a constitution with a lifetime president, his strangest and most confessional law, and calls Bolivia his beloved daughter. The mythology pauses here at the zenith: from this point every road leads down.
suggested_refs: Casa de la Libertad, Sucre, hall of the declaration
Decree of 11 August 1825 naming the República Bolívar
sources: https://historias-bolivia.blogspot.com/2018/10/la-asamblea-deliberante-de-1825-la.html
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Caracas, the last homecoming
stops.campa: Gran Colombia is cracking: Páez in revolt in Venezuela, Santander's lawyers against him in Bogotá. Bolívar comes home on 10 January 1827 to pardon Páez and be embraced by him under arches of triumph: statesmanship, or the beginning of surrender; the canon lets both stand. For six months he walks the streets of his and the republic's birth, ordering, endowing, remembering. On 5 July 1827 he sails from La Guaira for Bogotá. He will never see Caracas again; the city keeps the date like a wound.
suggested_refs: Tito Salas, the last departure from La Guaira (Casa Natal cycle)
sources: Fundación Empresas Polar, Diccionario de Historia de Venezuela
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Bucaramanga, the diary of the waiting lion
stops.campa: While the Convention of Ocaña tears at the constitution, Santander's men against his, Bolívar waits out the crisis for seventy days in the small town of Bucaramanga, forbidden by decorum to attend. His French aide Perú de Lacroix writes down everything: the Liberator at chess and at mass, his opinions of Napoleon and of priests, his rages, his insomnia, his tenderness, María Teresa remembered, Piar justified. The Diario de Bucaramanga becomes the canon's most intimate gospel: the hero pacing a provincial patio while his republic unstitches.
suggested_refs: Louis Perú de Lacroix, Diario de Bucaramanga (manuscript tradition)
Casa de Bolívar, Bucaramanga
sources: Louis Perú de Lacroix, Diario de Bucaramanga
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Bogotá, the night of September, 25 September 1828
stops.campa: Dictator now by the Organic Decree, Bolívar sleeps in the Palace of San Carlos. Past midnight the conspirators kill the sentries and break for his room; Manuela Sáenz, shaking him awake, arms him, delays him from dying sword in hand, and sends him out the window while she faces the blades alone and is beaten for it. Under the arch of the Carmen bridge the Liberator of half a world stands three hours in the water of the San Agustín, listening to the city hunt him. Rescued at dawn, he names her what the canon will call her forever.
stops.quote: You are the Liberatrix of the Liberator.
stops.quote_source: To Manuela Sáenz after the night of 25 September 1828 (O'Leary, Memorias; Manuela Sáenz's own accounts)
suggested_refs: Window of the Palacio de San Carlos, Bogotá, with its commemorative plaque
Portraits of Manuela Sáenz
sources: O'Leary, Memorias
Alfonso Rumazo González, Manuela Sáenz

stops.name: Bogotá, resignation and the road out
stops.campa: Venezuela secedes and proscribes him by name; his body is failing; the Congreso Admirable receives his final resignation. In his last message he lays down every power and keeps only the one title. On 8 May 1830 he rides out of Bogotá toward the river and the sea with a small escort and a chest of dwindling silver, the crowds silent, some weeping, his enemies scrawling triumph on the walls. The canon closes the gate of the capital behind him like the door of a tomb: the descent of the Magdalena begins.
stops.quote: Independence is the only benefit we have acquired, at the cost of all the rest.
stops.quote_source: Message to the Congreso Admirable, Bogotá, 20 January 1830
suggested_refs: Message to the Congreso Admirable, 20 January 1830
Quinta de Bolívar, Bogotá
sources: Doctrina del Libertador (Biblioteca Ayacucho)
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Cartagena, the blood of Abel
stops.campa: Down the Magdalena by boat to Turbaco and Cartagena, dying by stages, he waits for a ship to European exile that he will never board. Here the courier finds him: Sucre, the chosen one, the victor of Ayacucho, the heir, has been shot from ambush in the montaña of Berruecos on 4 June. Bolívar cries out the sentence the canon preserves as the epitaph of Gran Colombia, and those present say something in him breaks that no medicine afterward reaches: the future was Sucre, and the future has been murdered.
stops.quote: Holy God! The blood of Abel has been spilled!
stops.quote_source: On hearing of Sucre's assassination, Cartagena, 1 July 1830 (accounts of his aides; O'Leary, Memorias)
suggested_refs: Monument at Berruecos to Antonio José de Sucre
Walls of Cartagena
sources: O'Leary, Memorias
John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Barranquilla, 'he who serves a revolution ploughs the sea'
stops.campa: Wintering in the river towns of Soledad and Barranquilla, propped in a chair because lying down suffocates him, the Liberator writes to General Flores of Ecuador the letter the canon reads as his political last will: twenty years of rule distilled into six conclusions of terrifying clarity: America ungovernable, revolution a furrow in the water, the only sensible thing to emigrate, the country falling inevitably into the hands of tyrants of every color and then, perhaps, back to the Europeans. Despair itself is given the dignity of doctrine.
stops.quote: America is ungovernable for us. He who serves a revolution ploughs the sea.
stops.quote_source: Letter to General Juan José Flores, Barranquilla, 9 November 1830
suggested_refs: Letter to Flores, 9 November 1830 (facsimile tradition)
sources: Cartas del Libertador
Doctrina del Libertador (Biblioteca Ayacucho)

stops.name: Santa Marta, Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino, the last proclamation
stops.campa: On 1 December 1830 the brig Manuel lands him at Santa Marta, too weak to walk; a Spanish royalist, Joaquín de Mier, gives the dying republican his sugar estate of San Pedro Alejandrino: the canon underlines the charity of the old enemy. On 10 December, after receiving the last rites, Bolívar dictates from a red velvet armchair his final proclamation to the peoples of Colombia, forgiving, imploring union, offering his death itself as the last service. The doctors note that he rallies to dictate and sinks when it is done: the word was the last strength.
stops.quote: Colombians! You have witnessed my efforts to establish liberty where tyranny once reigned... If my death contributes to the ceasing of factions and the consolidation of the union, I shall go down in peace to my grave.
stops.quote_source: Last Proclamation of the Liberator, Hacienda de San Pedro Alejandrino, 10 December 1830
suggested_refs: Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino, Santa Marta
Original of the last proclamation (Archivo del Libertador, doc. 191)

stops.name: Santa Marta, death of the Liberator, 17 December 1830
stops.campa: At three minutes past one in the afternoon of 17 December 1830, eleven years to the day since he founded Colombia at Angostura, Simón Bolívar dies in a borrowed bed and a borrowed shirt at San Pedro Alejandrino, his fortune spent on the freedom of five nations. In his final wandering he calls for the crossing: vamos, vamos; la gente no nos quiere en esta tierra; muchachos, lleven mi equipaje a bordo de la fragata. The clock in the room is stopped at the hour; the oath of Monte Sacro is discharged in full, and the canon closes over him like the sea he ploughed.
stops.quote: How shall I ever get out of this labyrinth!
stops.quote_source: Attributed last words, San Pedro Alejandrino, December 1830 (accounts of his physicians and aides; the deathbed tradition)
